rationale: Covers all three key points without material error. (1) It says costly or illiquid holdings (wide spreads, shallow depth, closures, volatility) raise hedging costs and uncertainty, so quotes may widen. It also says liquid holdings and hedges can support competitive quotes. (2) It frames the spread as compensation for the cost and risk of providing immediacy, and says basket trading, financing, fees, operational constraints and inventory risk feed into quotes. It does not explicitly say market makers 'earn the spread', but the economic logic is clearly there. (3) It explains that historical volume reflects only past ETF trading. Volume misses current depth, underlying liquidity, and dealers' ability to hedge and process creation/redemption baskets. It notes a lightly traded ETF can still quote tightly, which implicitly captures that creation/redemption lets dealers adjust inventory beyond existing share trading. That point could have been stated more directly. Extra drivers (volatility, market closures, proxy hedging basis risk) are sound and allowed. No ranking of drivers, universal spread levels or promised capacity.
